records.title: Back up one folder every night and keep two weeks
records.summary: A nightly cron job archives one folder to a dated tar.gz and deletes archives older than fourteen days, so a restore is always a single file away.
records.problem: Backups that depend on remembering to run them are not backups. The folder that matters is usually one folder, and copying it by hand lasts about a week before it stops happening.
records.trigger: Cron, every night at 02:00 local time.

steps.action: Save the script as backup-folder.sh and make it executable
steps.detail: chmod +x backup-folder.sh. Edit SOURCE and DEST at the top; nothing else needs changing.

steps.action: Run it once by hand and confirm the archive opens
steps.detail: tar -tzf ~/Backups/Documents-YYYY-MM-DD.tar.gz lists the contents. If that fails, stop here and fix it before scheduling anything.

steps.action: Add the cron line
steps.detail: crontab -e, then: 0 2 * * * $HOME/bin/backup-folder.sh >> $HOME/.backup.log 2>&1

steps.action: Check the log the next morning
steps.detail: tail ~/.backup.log. One line per run, with the path it wrote.

prerequisites: A machine that is awake at the scheduled time. A laptop asleep at 02:00 skips the run.
Enough free space for fourteen compressed copies of the folder.
tar and cron, both present by default on macOS and Linux.
failureModes: The disk fills and tar writes a truncated archive. The script does not check free space, so watch the log and the archive sizes.
The source folder is renamed or moved, tar exits non-zero, and set -e stops the run. Nothing is deleted, but nothing is backed up either.
The archive sits on the same disk as the source, so one dead drive loses both. Point DEST at an external volume or a synced folder.
cron runs with a minimal environment. Use absolute paths, and test the way cron will see it: env -i /bin/bash $HOME/bin/backup-folder.sh

payload.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Nightly archive of one folder. Keeps the last 14 days, deletes the rest.
set -euo pipefail

SOURCE="$HOME/Documents"
DEST="$HOME/Backups"
KEEP_DAYS=14

mkdir -p "$DEST"
NAME="$(basename "$SOURCE")"
ARCHIVE="$DEST/$NAME-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).tar.gz"

tar --create --gzip --file "$ARCHIVE" --directory "$(dirname "$SOURCE")" "$NAME"
find "$DEST" -name "$NAME-*.tar.gz" -type f -mtime +"$KEEP_DAYS" -delete

echo "$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S) wrote $ARCHIVE"

records.title: Tell a chat channel when a site goes down, once
records.summary: A five minute cron check posts to a chat webhook only when a site changes state, so an outage announces itself once and the recovery announces itself once.
records.problem: Uptime checks that post on every failed poll turn a two hour outage into twenty four identical messages, and people mute the channel. The useful signal is the transition, not the poll.

steps.action: Create an incoming webhook in the chat tool and copy the URL
steps.detail: Any service that accepts a JSON body with a text field works the same way.

steps.action: Put the webhook URL in the environment, not in the script
steps.detail: The script reads SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL and exits with a message if it is missing.

steps.action: Set URL at the top and run it twice by hand
steps.detail: The first run records the state and stays quiet. Point it at a URL that fails to watch the alert fire.

steps.action: Add the cron line
steps.detail: */5 * * * * SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL=https://... $HOME/bin/uptime.sh

prerequisites: A webhook URL from the chat tool.
curl, present by default on macOS and most Linux images.
A writable /tmp for the state file.
failureModes: The checking machine loses its own network. Everything looks down and the alert cannot be sent anyway. Run this somewhere other than the machine you are watching.
/tmp is cleared on reboot, the state resets to up, and a still down site alerts a second time. Move STATE_FILE somewhere persistent if that matters.
The site returns 200 with an error page. This checks the status code only.
A redirect returns 301 and reads as down. Add -L to the curl call if redirects are expected.

payload.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Check one URL. Post to chat only when the state changes, so a long
# outage does not repeat the same message every five minutes.
set -euo pipefail

URL="https://example.com"
WEBHOOK="${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL:?set SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL in the environment}"
STATE_FILE="/tmp/uptime-$(printf '%s' "$URL" | cksum | cut -d' ' -f1).state"

code="$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 10 "$URL" || echo 000)"
if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then now="up"; else now="down"; fi

was="$(cat "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo up)"
printf '%s' "$now" > "$STATE_FILE"

if [ "$now" = "$was" ]; then
  exit 0
fi

if [ "$now" = "down" ]; then
  text="$URL is down. HTTP $code."
else
  text="$URL is back. HTTP $code."
fi

curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "$(printf '{"text":"%s"}' "$text")" "$WEBHOOK" > /dev/null

records.title: File every receipt out of the inbox automatically
records.summary: One Gmail filter labels anything that looks like a receipt or an invoice and archives it, so purchases stay searchable in one place and out of the inbox.
records.problem: Receipts arrive constantly, are read once, and are needed twice a year. Left in the inbox they are noise. Deleted, they are gone at tax time.
records.trigger: Every incoming message, evaluated by Gmail on arrival.

steps.action: Create a label called Receipts
Import the filter
steps.detail: Settings > Filters and blocked addresses > Import filters, upload the file below, then select the filter and create it.

steps.action: Apply it to existing mail once
steps.detail: Search the same terms, select all, apply the label and archive. A filter only sees new mail.

steps.action: Watch it for a week and tighten the terms
steps.detail: Anything wrongly filed tells you which word is too broad. no-reply is the usual culprit.

prerequisites: A Gmail or Google Workspace account.
Five minutes to read what the search matches before turning it on.
failureModes: The word invoice appears in a thread that matters and it is archived unread. Search label:Receipts to find it, then narrow the terms.
Receipts that use none of these words are missed. Add senders as you notice them.
The filter does not touch mail that arrived before it existed. Step 3 exists for that reason.
shouldNeverSpam keeps these out of spam, which also means a fake receipt stays in the inbox. Read before clicking, always.

payload.content:
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'?>
<feed xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom' xmlns:apps='http://schemas.google.com/apps/2006'>
  <title>Mail Filters</title>
  <entry>
    <category term='filter'></category>
    <title>Receipts</title>
    <apps:property name='hasTheWord' value='subject:(receipt OR invoice OR "order confirmation" OR "your order") OR from:(billing OR receipts OR invoices OR no-reply)'/>
    <apps:property name='label' value='Receipts'/>
    <apps:property name='shouldArchive' value='true'/>
    <apps:property name='shouldNeverSpam' value='true'/>
    <apps:property name='sizeOperator' value='s_sl'/>
    <apps:property name='sizeUnit' value='s_smb'/>
  </entry>
</feed>

records.title: Build, test and deploy on every push to main
records.summary: A GitHub Actions workflow installs, tests and builds on every push to main and then runs one publish step, cancelling an older run when a newer push arrives.
records.problem: Deploying by hand from a laptop means the deployed thing was built on that laptop, with whatever happened to be installed that day, and two people deploying at once race each other.
records.trigger: A push to the main branch.

steps.action: Save the workflow at .github/workflows/deploy.yml
Put the deploy credential in repository secrets as DEPLOY_TOKEN
steps.detail: Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions. Never in the workflow file.

steps.action: Write scripts/publish.sh so it is the only step that touches production
steps.detail: Keeping the publish in one script means it can still be run by hand in an emergency.

steps.action: Push a trivial change and watch the run
steps.detail: The Actions tab shows every step. A green run that skipped the tests is not a green run: check that npm test actually ran.

prerequisites: A repository on GitHub with Actions enabled.
A package.json with a build script. Tests are optional: --if-present skips cleanly when there are none.
A deploy credential that can be revoked on its own without rotating anything else.
failureModes: cancel-in-progress cancels a run that was already mid publish. Make publish.sh safe to run twice, or drop the concurrency block.
npm ci fails when package-lock.json is out of date with package.json. Commit the lockfile.
The build passes on the runner and fails on a developer machine, or the reverse. The runner is the source of truth from now on.
A secret is only masked in logs when it matches exactly. Do not echo credentials, even partially.

payload.content:
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# One deploy at a time. A newer push cancels an older run.
concurrency:
  group: deploy
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test --if-present
      - run: npm run build
      - name: Publish
        run: ./scripts/publish.sh
        env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}

records.title: Reclaim disk space from Docker every Sunday
records.summary: A weekly cron line prunes Docker images, containers, networks and build cache untouched for seven days, and deliberately leaves volumes alone so data survives.
records.problem: Docker keeps every layer it has ever pulled. On a build machine that is tens of gigabytes within a month, and the first symptom is a build failing on a full disk at an inconvenient hour.

steps.action: See what would go first
steps.detail: docker system df shows reclaimable space per category.

steps.action: Add the line to root's crontab
steps.detail: sudo crontab -e. Talking to the docker socket needs root or membership of the docker group.

steps.action: Check the log after the first Sunday
steps.detail: tail /var/log/docker-prune.log shows what was deleted and how much space came back.

prerequisites: Docker installed, and permission to talk to the daemon.
A writable /var/log, or a different path in the line.
Nothing on the machine that depends on an image it cannot pull again.
failureModes: --all removes images with no running container, including one a stopped container needs at its next start. Drop --all to keep tagged images.
An air gapped machine cannot re-pull what was pruned. Do not run this there.
The until filter is relative to image creation, not last use. An old base image in daily use is still removed and pulled again.
Volumes are untouched by design. Adding --volumes to this line deletes database data.

payload.content:
# Sunday 04:00. Removes images, containers, networks and build cache
# untouched for a week. Volumes are left alone on purpose.
0 4 * * 0 /usr/bin/docker system prune --all --force --filter "until=168h" >> /var/log/docker-prune.log 2>&1

records.title: Post every form response to a chat channel
records.summary: An Apps Script trigger on the responses spreadsheet posts each new form submission to a chat channel as a readable message, so the people who act on it never open the sheet.
records.problem: A form writes a row and nobody sees it. The team either checks the sheet out of habit or finds out days later that someone was waiting on them.
records.trigger: A form submission, through the spreadsheet's on form submit trigger.

steps.action: Open the responses spreadsheet, then Extensions > Apps Script
Paste the script and save
Add SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL under Project Settings > Script properties
steps.detail: Script properties keep the webhook out of the code and out of version control.

steps.action: Add the trigger
steps.detail: Triggers > Add trigger > function onFormSubmit > event source From spreadsheet > event type On form submit. Authorize when prompted.

steps.action: Submit the form once as a test
steps.detail: Executions in the Apps Script sidebar shows the run and any error.

prerequisites: A Google Form whose responses go to a spreadsheet.
An incoming webhook URL from the chat tool.
Permission to authorize a script on the account that owns the form.
failureModes: The trigger is attached to the form instead of the spreadsheet and e.namedValues is empty. It must be From spreadsheet.
A long free text answer makes the message unreadable in chat. Post the questions that matter rather than all of them.
The webhook is revoked and every run fails quietly. muteHttpExceptions keeps the row from being lost, so check Executions occasionally.
Apps Script has daily quotas on UrlFetchApp. A form taking thousands of responses a day needs a different approach.
